title: Lucy Gray: occasion and source
short: Written at Goslar in 1799 and published in Lyrical Ballads (1800); based on Dorothy's story of a child lost in a snowstorm near Halifax.
body: Wordsworth's Fenwick note says the poem 'was founded on a circumstance told me by my sister' of a little girl near Halifax in Yorkshire who was lost in a snowstorm; her footsteps were traced by her parents to the middle of a lock on the canal, and no other vestige of her could be found. He added that the treatment and 'spiritualizing' of the character might be contrasted with George Crabbe's 'matter-of-fact' handling of similar subjects. The subtitle 'or, Solitude' names the theme; Henry Crabb Robinson reports that Wordsworth meant to exhibit 'entire solitude'. Wordsworth later placed the poem among the 'Poems referring to the Period of Childhood'.

anchor: And, when I crossed the wild
title: ballad stanza
short: Sixteen quatrains in ballad (common) measure, alternating four- and three-beat lines, rhyming abab.
body: The traditional ballad stanza suits the poem's folk-tale manner: a narrator who has heard the story ('Oft I had heard'), dialogue in direct speech, a stark event, and a closing legend. Lyrical Ballads presented such forms as experiments in using the language of ordinary people. 'The wild' means wild, uncultivated country, a moor; the speaker claims once to have glimpsed the child, so the frame both vouches for her reality and prepares for the ghostly ending.

sources.cite: Wordsworth, Preface to Lyrical Ballads (1800; revised 1802)
William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 2 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and notes to the poem

title: the solitary child
short: Lucy has 'No mate, no comrade', living on a wide moor: solitude is her nature, not merely her situation.
body: Crabb Robinson reports Wordsworth's saying that his aim was to exhibit 'entire solitude'. The child is described in the language of nature: 'The sweetest thing that ever grew / Beside a human door', as if she were a flower or tree at the edge of the human world. The phrase 'human door' marks that boundary between the household and the moor, which she will cross.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 2 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and notes to the poem
Geoffrey H. Hartman, Wordsworth's Poetry 1787-1814 (New Haven, 1964)

title: 'Beside a human door'
short: She 'grew' beside the house as a plant grows: the line makes her half a natural creature.
body: The verb 'grew' and the adjective 'human' are both unexpected: we expect 'the sweetest flower that ever grew' and 'beside a cottage door'. By calling the door 'human', Wordsworth implies that Lucy herself belongs partly outside the human order, to the moor and its creatures. The next stanza confirms this: the fawn and the hare may still be seen, but Lucy 'Will never more be seen', so she is grouped with wild animals rather than with people.

sources.cite: Geoffrey H. Hartman, Wordsworth's Poetry 1787-1814 (New Haven, 1964)
William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 2 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and notes to the poem

title: the fawn and the hare
short: The wild creatures of the moor survive, but Lucy does not: the stanza announces her loss before the story begins.
body: This stanza anticipates the ending, telling the reader at once that Lucy 'Will never more be seen', so the narrative that follows is read as a tragedy foretold. The animals also prepare for the comparison of Lucy with the 'mountain roe' (l. 25).

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 2 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and notes to the poem

title: minster
greek: Old English mynster, from Latin monasterium
short: A large or important church, originally a monastery church; the minster clock tells the time to the town below.
body: The word comes ultimately from Latin monasterium and is used in the north of England for great churches such as York Minster. The hour matters: it is only two in the afternoon, and Lucy is confident of returning before dark.

title: the afternoon moon
short: Lucy points to the moon in the daytime sky, a detail Wordsworth thought only a child of lonely places would notice.
body: Crabb Robinson recorded that Wordsworth meant the child to be seen 'observing the day-moon, which no town or village girl would ever notice'. The moon thus characterizes Lucy as a creature attuned to the moor. It also introduces an ominous note: the moon is already up while she expects to light her mother home through the snow, and the storm comes 'before its time' (l. 29). Moon imagery recurs across the Lucy poems, most strikingly in 'Strange fits of passion'.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 2 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and notes to the poem

title: hook and faggot-band
short: The father cuts with his billhook the cord binding a bundle of firewood.
body: A faggot is a bundle of sticks for fuel, and the faggot-band the twisted withy or cord tying it; the 'hook' is a billhook, a curved woodman's blade. The gesture is brisk and unreflective: the father sends the child and goes on with his work ('He plied his work'). The poem does not blame him, but the everyday task, set against the coming storm, sharpens the pathos.

title: the mountain roe
short: The roe deer: Lucy is livelier than a young deer on the hills, an image with biblical overtones of swiftness and grace.
body: The roe is a small deer. In the Song of Solomon the beloved is 'like a roe or a young hart' leaping on the mountains (2:9, 2:17), and 'swift as a roe' is a scriptural commonplace (2 Samuel 2:18). The comparison continues the identification of Lucy with the creatures of the moor. 'Not blither' (not more cheerful) is an ironic understatement, given what follows.

title: wanton
short: Here 'playful, frolicsome, unrestrained', with no moral sense: her feet kick up the powdery snow in play.
body: 'Wanton' originally meant undisciplined or ungoverned, and in older poetry is often used of children and young animals at play (OED). The image of the snow rising 'like smoke' is precise and visual, and the playful energy of the stanza marks the last moment of ordinary life before 'The storm came on before its time'. The word thus carries, in retrospect, a hint of carelessness or heedlessness, though the poem does not blame the child.

title: the storm and the search
short: Lucy loses her way and never reaches the town; her parents search all night 'shouting far and wide' with neither sound nor sight to guide them.
body: The catastrophe is told with almost no detail: 'She wandered up and down'. The parents' night search is equally bare. The poem's restraint follows the ballad tradition of telling events without commentary. The phrase 'neither sound nor sight / To serve them for a guide' reverses Lucy's mission: she was to carry a light to guide her mother, and now the parents have no guide to find her.

title: furlong
short: An eighth of a mile (220 yards), originally the length of a furrow in a common field.
body: From the hill at daybreak the parents see the wooden bridge, very close to home: Lucy was lost almost within reach of the house. The measurement increases the pathos. In the Fenwick note the real child's footprints ended in the middle of a canal lock; Wordsworth changes the lock to a 'bridge of wood' and 'plank', a more rural setting.

anchor: In heaven we all shall meet
title: 'In heaven we all shall meet'
short: The parents' pious resignation, just before the mother sees the footprints and hope revives.
body: The cry expresses the conventional Christian consolation for a lost child; it comes at the very moment when the mother spies 'The print of Lucy's feet', so faith and the physical trace are juxtaposed. The following stanzas, tracking the 'footmarks small' through hedge and field and along the wall, are among the most suspenseful in Wordsworth, a slow repetition ('one by one') that builds towards the empty plank.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 2 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and notes to the poem

title: 'And further there were none!'
short: The footprints stop in the middle of the plank. The poem never says that Lucy drowned.
body: Wordsworth's source ended with the footsteps stopping in the middle of a canal lock and no trace of the child afterwards; the poem keeps the bare trace and adds the plank. The footprints simply end, leaving a mystery that the closing stanzas exploit. This is the 'spiritualizing' that Wordsworth contrasted with Crabbe's realism: by never describing the death, he lets the child pass out of the human world rather than die in it. Readers differ on whether the effect is consoling, suggesting her absorption into nature, or uncanny and bleak.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 2 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and notes to the poem
Geoffrey H. Hartman, Wordsworth's Poetry 1787-1814 (New Haven, 1964)

title: the closing legend
short: Local belief that Lucy is still alive, a 'living child' seen on the moor: the story becomes a ghost-legend.
body: The last two stanzas move from narrative to rumour ('some maintain'), reporting a folk belief without endorsing it. The present tense ('she trips along', 'sings') contrasts with the past tense of the story, so Lucy enters a timeless state. Many readers find the ending eerie rather than comforting; others see it as Wordsworth's characteristic transformation of loss into enduring presence in the landscape. The opening frame ('Oft I had heard', 'I chanced to see') suggests that the narrator himself may have seen her spirit.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 2 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and notes to the poem
Geoffrey H. Hartman, Wordsworth's Poetry 1787-1814 (New Haven, 1964)

title: the solitary song
short: The last image: her song merges with the wind, so that voice and nature become indistinguishable.
body: 'Never looks behind' recalls her obedient errand and the moving forward of a spirit; her 'solitary song' fulfils the subtitle 'Solitude'. The wind that 'whistles' may be heard as her song, or her song as the wind; the ambiguity completes the poem's movement of Lucy out of the human household into the moor. Readers may compare the Highland reaper's 'solitary' song in 'The Solitary Reaper' (1807).
